{"path": "/home/user/clio-agent/.cloud-run/f17/ws-f17-docs/design/sdk/plugins-and-composition.md", "size_bytes": 17579, "content": "# CLIO Agent Plugins and Composition

Oct 6, 2026 · @Jaime

## Purpose

Every capability in CLIO, and every line of its main prompt, should have exactly one home: the plugin it belongs to. Agents never own content. They select plugins, and the system composes tools, hooks, catalogs and prompt text from that selection.

Today the same pdf skill is maintained in three agents and the a2a skill in four, so a single fix has to be copied everywhere. The standard agent's main prompt has the same problem: its general guidelines are copied into every other agent and drift apart.

This document covers the plugin model only: the plugin standard, how agents are composed from plugins, how the main prompt is composed, and how plugins evolve per user. The Python SDK that implements this model and the design for remote agents each have their own document.

## Starting point and what changed

The Sept 17 planning session replaced the Markdown blueprint system with Python-defined agents on the Agent Plugins 1.0.0 standard. Most of that holds; the composition model is new, and one assumption about external plugin sources was dropped.

| Sept 17 decision | Status now |
| --- | --- |
| Agents are authored in Python; users kept getting the AGENT.md format wrong with no feedback | Holds |
| Python is the authoring surface; a frozen `spec()` stored at install is the runtime contract | Holds |
| Trust split: pip-installed plugins are trusted, git-installed ones need an explicit trust step | Holds |
| Agent Plugins 1.0.0 portable core plus one `ai.iowarp.clio` namespace | Holds, with the gap that the core has no composition (see Plugin standard) |
| "Blueprint" disappears; install a plugin, pick one of its agents | Replaced: an agent is a composition of plugins, not something a plugin ships whole |
| Delete the AGENT.md loader and legacy `clio-pack.yaml` path in one change, no dual loader | Holds |
| Agents declare capability requirements and preferences; operators resolve providers | Holds |
| Plugin-qualified tool names avoid collisions | Replaced: a collision is a resolution error |
| Rewriting other repositories' plugin layouts to match ours | Dropped: any repository is just a source of servers and skills, and none gets special treatment |

New since Sept 17: agents as plugin sets with packs and deltas, complete-by-default agents, the composed main prompt, coexistence rules for competing plugins, and per-user self-optimizing plugins.

## Plugin standard

The plugin is the unit of everything: distribution, trust, composition and evolution. CLIO uses [Agent Plugins 1.0.0](https://agent-plugins.org/specification) as the package format and defines composition itself, because the standard does not.

**What the core gives us.** `plugin.json` permits only ten top-level fields: `$schema`, `name`, `version`, `description`, `author`, `homepage`, `repository`, `license`, `keywords` and `extensions`. The portable components are `skills/` in the Agent Skills format and `mcp.json` for MCP servers. Client-specific content goes under a reverse-domain namespace, both as a key in `extensions` and as a top-level directory, and the namespace owner defines its validation.

**What the core lacks.** There is no field for dependencies, bundles or requirements on other plugins, nothing about marketplaces, and no hooks, agents or commands in the core. All of that is ours to define inside `ai.iowarp.clio`.

**What a plugin can contribute.** A plugin is never only skills. It may contribute any of:

- MCP servers (portable core)
- Skills (portable core)
- Hooks
- A2UI catalogs and other catalog access
- Defined subagents and specific peers, meaning external agents the plugin needs
- Commands
- Custom Python tools
- Prompt fragments (see Composed main prompt)
- Providers such as structured-file providers, and flows (orchestration programs such as ReAct, a council or a campaign)
- Dependencies on other plugins, either pack membership or hard requirements

**Layout.**

```text
pdf/
├── plugin.json          # $schema pinned to 1.0.0; extensions: { "ai.iowarp.clio": { ... } }
├── skills/              # portable
├── mcp.json             # portable
└── ai.iowarp.clio/
    ├── plugin.py        # identity, requirements, metadata only
    ├── tools/           # Python tools
    ├── hooks/           # hooks
    ├── subagents/       # defined subagents
    ├── commands/        # commands
    ├── flows/           # orchestration flows
    ├── prompt/          # fragments
    └── a2ui/            # catalogs
```

**Sources.** Servers and skills can come from any repository or registry. No source is special; a plugin references what it uses, and the resolver fetches it.

## External plugins and trust

CLIO loads plugins published in other formats, such as the Claude Code plugin layout, by importing them at install into the same internal plugin record. There is one importer per format and a single loader in the runtime.

An external plugin brings what it has and nothing more: MCP servers and skills, and sometimes defined subagents or commands, which stay with that plugin. It has no prompt fragments or requirements, the same as any plugin that does not need them. Once imported, it is validated, resolved, placed in packs and agents, and removed from the + menu like a native plugin.

Learned copies work the same way. `hdf5_personal` declares `evolved_from` the external `hdf5`, `check_updates` watches that source, and `rebase` starts from its latest version. When a source publishes no versions, the import pins by commit hash so an upstream change is still well defined.

| Source or change | Trust |
| --- | --- |
| pip-installed package | Trusted by construction, as pip already is |
| Git repository or external marketplace | Explicit trust step at install |
| Update that changes executable parts (server commands, Python tools, hooks) | Trust step again before it applies |
| Update that changes only text (skills, fragments) | Applies to the next session without a new trust step |
| Personal evolved fork | Inherits its upstream's trust, since the optimizer never touches executable parts |

## Agents as plugin sets

An agent is a flow, an identity and a set of plugins. A flow is the agent's orchestration program; the default is ReAct, and the orchestration document covers the rest. Remove every plugin and what is left is a chatbot with no tools. The standard agent's pdf, docs, excel, a2a, shell and subagent capabilities are all plugins on the root agent, not subagents.

**Packs.** A pack is a plugin whose content is only membership in other plugins. `documents` is pdf, docx, xlsx and pptx. An agent can carry the whole pack or any two of its members; both resolve the same way.

**Shipped agents in Python.** A new class means a new identity. New capabilities arrive as packs, which keeps the class hierarchy shallow and makes "why does my agent have this?" answerable.

```python
manufacturing = Pack("manufacturing", [abaqus, tosca, plato, am_process])

class Factorio(ScienceAgent):
    id = "factorio"
    role = "a manufacturing and topology optimization agent"
    plugins = ScienceAgent.plugins + [manufacturing]
```

**User agents as deltas.** The + menu lets a user add or remove plugins, rename the result and save it to their own marketplace. It is stored as a parent plus a delta, never a flattened list, so a fix to pdf in standard reaches every descendant.

```yaml
id: my-personal-default
extends: clio/standard@^1
remove: [xlsx]
```

**Resolution.** Expand packs, apply additions, then apply removals. Removing xlsx works even though it arrived through `documents`. A saved agent follows its parent within the major version.

**Complete by default.** Every shipped agent works out of the box. Factorio ships with both Abaqus and Plato even though they compete. Removing plugins is an optimization of context, knowledge or startup cost, never a repair, so a user can never assemble a stack that does not work.

**Membership versus requirement.** Pack membership is removable: dropping plato from manufacturing is fine. A hard requirement takes its dependents with it: removing shell when the github plugin requires it is allowed and removes github as well, and the UI shows what else goes. Requirements are declared per plugin.

**Sessions are pinned.** A session freezes its resolved plugin set at start. Parent updates and newly evolved personal plugins apply to the next session. Adding or removing a plugin inside a live session produces a new resolved set and a new prompt for that session.

**Traceability.** The UI shows where each plugin came from: core, standard, science, a pack, or the user.

## Coexistence rules

Complete-by-default agents load competing plugins side by side, so the resolver has to keep them from colliding or contradicting each other.

- **Tool name collisions are errors.** If two plugins expose the same tool name, resolution fails with a message naming both plugins. Authors are pushed toward specific names such as `plato_optimize`, and the model sees readable names.
- **Hooks run from child to parent**, so pdf's hooks run before the science agent's. The SDK can adjust order with `before=` and `after=` referencing other hook ids. A cycle is a resolution error. Since every hook has an id, ordering can be exposed in the UI later.
- **Fragments describe, they never claim exclusivity.** The Abaqus fragment says what Abaqus does; it never says to use Abaqus for all topology optimization. Choosing between alternatives belongs to the pack's own fragment or to the user.
- **Everything-on stays cheap.** Tools load deferred, with only names and descriptions in context until a tool is used, and MCP servers start lazily on first use. That keeps complete-by-default affordable and makes removal a real optimization rather than a necessity.

## Composed main prompt

The main prompt is assembled from fragments contributed by the agent and its plugins, in a fixed sequence of sections. No agent carries a hand-written copy of shared guidance.

1. **Identity**: "You are {agent.name}, {agent.role}." Owned by the agent; a child agent replaces it.
2. **Operating guidelines**: universal behavior, owned by a `core` plugin that every agent carries.
3. **Rendering**: what CLIO can display (LaTeX, citations, typed parts, A2UI components), generated from the same catalog the UI renders from. This closes the formatting gap identified on Sept 17.
4. **Capabilities**: one fragment per plugin that needs one.
5. **Domain**: science, manufacturing and similar framing.

A fragment is a small file in its plugin's `prompt/` directory:

```markdown
---
id: shell.prefer-gh
section: capabilities
when: { tools: [shell] }
---
When working with GitHub, check whether `gh` is authenticated and prefer it.
```

**Rules.**

- **A guideline lives with the capability it describes.** "Prefer gh" belongs to the shell plugin, so every agent with a shell gets it and an agent without one never sees an instruction it cannot follow.
- **Fragments carry only what the model cannot infer** from tool schemas and skill descriptions. A paragraph restating what the pdf tools do does not belong. The validator enforces a soft size budget per fragment (a warning above 150 tokens to start), since the root prompt grows with every plugin.
- **Fragments stand alone.** None refers to another ("as described above"). Joint guidance for two plugins uses `when: { plugins: [a, b] }` and should be rare.
- **Fragments have ids**, so agent deltas drop or replace them the same way they add or remove plugins.
- **Templating is minimal**: agent identity and environment variables only, no logic, so a scientist can still read and edit a fragment.
- **Ordering is deterministic**: sections first, then plugin resolution order. Stable sections lead, so toggling a plugin only invalidates the prompt cache from the capabilities section down.
- **The UI shows the composed prompt** with each fragment attributed to its plugin.

**Subagents.** Capability plugins attach to the agent that carries them; they are not subagents. There are two kinds of subagent. A general subagent is launched by the agent at runtime with only a task prompt, such as another CLIO told to find a needle, possibly a standard agent on a different model; that ability comes from one delegation plugin. A defined subagent, such as a planner, is shipped by the plugin it belongs to and arrives or leaves with that plugin. A subagent's prompt is composed the same way from the plugins it is given, so a pdf fragment written once serves the root and any subagent carrying pdf.

**Migrating standard's prompt.** The current prompt is cut apart: the identity line stays with the agent, universal guidelines move to `core`, and each capability paragraph moves into the plugin it describes.

**Task guidance.** The task lifecycle snippet (`clio.runtime.tasks`), which teaches handles, waits and Stop versus cancellation to every task-capable root and child, becomes a `core` fragment, so it is written once and reaches every agent.

## Self-optimizing plugins

Plugins evolve per user from their own sessions, on a schedule, and running sessions never change underneath the user. Lineage lives on plugins, not on agent classes, so agents stay shallow while plugins carry their history.

**Lineage and the override slot.** An optimization run produces a personal fork such as `pdf_personal`, declared `evolved_from: pdf@1.5.0`. The user layer then applies one rule: wherever `pdf` appears in any agent, this user gets `pdf_personal`. When both marketplaces are available, the fork maps onto the original's slot, so every agent that includes pdf picks up the improvement without being edited.

**Timing.** The optimizer runs periodically (daily or weekly), offline or when the user triggers it. It publishes a new version of `pdf_personal`, and the next Factorio session resolves `pdf` to it. A running session keeps its pinned version.

**The cycle is one agent's job.** Nothing about it is mechanical. Each run regenerates the fork from the latest upstream plus the accumulated lessons rather than editing last period's fork, so an upstream release is absorbed by the rebase step instead of by a merge.

[embedded content: Optimization cycle with two gates\]

A failure at gate 1 points to the upstream change; a failure at gate 2 points to the new lessons. Neither publishes.

**Lessons are discrete units.** Each lesson records what changed, which component it touches, and the evidence behind it, such as the session and failure it came from. The fork is an upstream version plus an ordered lesson list, so every published version is reproducible. This gives the agent clean units to reason about rather than a block of edited prose.

**Revert and promotion are agent tasks too.** A gate failure or a user request triggers a revert: the agent decides which lesson to drop, rebuilds without it and gates again. A lesson that many users' forks share can be proposed as a change to upstream `pdf`.

**What may evolve.** Text and parameters only: skills, prompt fragments and configuration. MCP server code and executable hooks are never rewritten by the optimizer, since that crosses the trust boundary set for plugin code.

**The gate.** The validator plus the plugin's evals, run on both upstream and the candidate. Learning from negatives can overfit, and without a gate a fork can quietly get worse. This depends on the benchmarks and evals work already scoped for 1.0.

## Decisions and open items

| Area | Decision |
| --- | --- |
| Package format | Agent Plugins 1.0.0 core plus the `ai.iowarp.clio` namespace |
| Composition | Defined by CLIO in the namespace, since the core has none |
| Agent | A flow, an identity and a set of plugins |
| Capabilities | Plugins on the agent that carries them, not subagents |
| Subagents | General subagents come from one delegation plugin; defined subagents ship with the plugin they belong to |
| Grouping | Packs; a new agent class only for a new identity |
| User agents | Parent plus delta, saved to the user's marketplace from the + menu |
| Defaults | Complete by default; removal is optimization |
| Dependencies | Pack membership is removable; hard requirements are declared per plugin, and removing one also removes its dependents |
| Tool names | A collision is a resolution error |
| Hooks | Child to parent, adjustable with `before`/`after`, cycles are errors |
| Cost | Deferred tool loading and lazy server startup |
| Main prompt | Composed from fragments in five fixed sections, attributed in the UI |
| Fragments | Live with their capability, stand alone, have ids, stay small |
| Sessions | Pinned at start; updates apply to the next session |
| Evolution | Periodic, agent-driven, regenerated from upstream plus lessons, gated after rebase and after new lessons |
| Evolvable parts | Skills, prompt fragments and configuration only |
| External agents | An external-agents pack (a2a, acp, academy) provides discovery and one fragment; specific peers are declared by the plugins that need them; agents own only their exposure |

**Deferred by design.**

- **Evals live in the plugin's repository** and are not parsed by CLIO. The optimization gate runs them; the plugin format does not need to describe them.
- **The lesson record schema and the personal marketplace come later**, in the optimization campaign. This design only leaves room for them: `evolved_from`, the override slot and session pinning.

Oct 22, 2026 · @Jaime

## Summary

Choosing the model becomes a first-class part of CLIO 1.0, on the same footing as plugins and flows. Today a whole session tree runs on one model: the person picks it, and every subagent, flow call and workflow step inherits it unchanged. After this change, every place that starts model work can name a model, CLIO itself can choose one, and both the person and the agent can see what each connected account has left.

The design has four parts that share one data source:

1. **The fleet.** One registry of connected accounts and the models each serves, joined with the capability records CLIO already keeps (context, tools, vision, price).
2. **Usage.** One adapter per provider reports windows, percent used, reset times and remaining balance. Claude and Codex subscriptions, OpenRouter credit, API-key accounts and local endpoints all report in the same shape.
3. **Selection.** `Prefers` and `Requires` finally drive model choice, and spawns, `ctx.call`, workflow steps and RLM leaves accept an explicit `model`. Every choice is checked against the fleet and recorded; a preference that cannot be met is reported, never silently replaced.
4. **Surfaces.** Agent tools (`list_models`, `usage`) and the UI from [issue #1802](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-agent/issues/1802): a Usage view of every account, and a hover readout under the chat box for the account in use. The widget idea comes from [quotabubble](https://github.com/izzet/quotabubble).

## Current state

Checked against `claude/sdk-plugins-flows` at `b4cf79b8`. The pieces exist, but nothing connects declarations to the model a session actually uses.

| Piece | State at the base | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Session model | A dict `{provider_id, model_id}` set at creation from the request or from session defaults | `gact/routes/session_creation.py:49` |
| Child sessions | Copy `parent.model` exactly; spawn tools, `ctx.call` and workflow steps have no model argument | `gact/spawn_context.py:150` |
| Declarations | `Requires` (tool calling, vision, context and output tokens) and `Prefers` (model, provider, effort) on `Agent`, `Subagent` and `Plugin` | `sdk/model.py` |
| Use of declarations | `Requires` is unioned across plugins into the resolution. `Prefers` is recorded and never read when a session is created | `plugins/resolve.py:556`, `gact/agents/resolution.py:205` |
| Providers | 19 presets including `claude_code`, `codex`, `openrouter`, `anthropic`, `openai`, `vllm`, `ollama`, `argonne_sophia`, `argonne_metis`, `amsc_mag` | `providers/catalog.py` |
| Capabilities | Model, Endpoint and Deployment records, every field a `Fact` with source and time; `TokenPricing` for list and endpoint prices | `providers/capabilities/records.py` |
| Secondary roles | One, `summarizer`, configured by file or environment | `lm/secondary.py:15` |
| Agent-facing tools | Only `refresh_provider_models` (the update-models skill). No tool lists accounts, models or usage | `core` plugin `tools/runtime.py` |
| Claude usage | The Agent SDK's rate-limit events carry `utilization`, `resets_at` and the limit type; CLIO reads them only to classify a rejection | `providers/claude_code_plan_limit.py` |
| Codex usage | A usage limit is detected by matching error text | `providers/codex/direct_engine.py:399`, `codex/errors.py` |
| Recovery | Plan-limit and safety errors suggest `switch_model`, but nothing performs it | `providers/claude_code_plan_limit.py:192` |

The Codex text match breaks the existing rule against keyword-matching prose where a structured field exists, and is replaced in Phase 2.

## Design: the fleet

The fleet is a read model over what CLIO already stores, not a new store. It joins three things: the person's connected accounts, the models each account can serve, and the capability records for each model and endpoint.

**Account.** One configured provider instance with its credential: a Claude subscription through the Agent SDK, a ChatGPT subscription through Codex OAuth, an OpenRouter key, an Anthropic API key, a vLLM router on a homelab, an Argonne endpoint. An account has an id, a provider preset, a billing kind (`subscription`, `credit`, `metered`, `free`) and a health state from the existing provider probe.

**Fleet entry.** One `(account, model)` pair, carrying:

- the combined capabilities from `providers/capabilities/combine.py`, so `Requires` can be checked without a new code path;
- price per million input and output tokens from `TokenPricing`, with its source, and zero for free endpoints;
- the latest usage snapshot for the account (next section);
- an `available` flag that is false when the account is unhealthy, exhausted or the model is not served.

**Freshness.** Model lists come from the existing discovery and `refresh_provider_models`. Usage is refreshed by its adapters. Every fleet field keeps its `Fact` provenance, so the UI and the agent see where a value came from and how old it is.

**One owner.** `GET /v1/fleet` serves the UI, the agent tools read the same function in-process, and the selection logic uses the same function. There is no second model list anywhere, and the hard-coded fallback lists that remain are deleted.

## Design: usage

**One protocol.** Each provider preset may ship a usage adapter, following quotabubble's `Provider` protocol shape. It returns a `UsageSnapshot`: a list of windows (name, percent used, resets at), an optional balance (amount, currency, limit), the time observed, and the source. A provider with no notion of quota returns `unmetered` rather than nothing, so the UI never shows a blank.

**Two ways to learn usage.** Passive capture reads what calls already return, at no extra cost. Polling asks the provider when the account is idle, every 5 minutes by default. Where both exist, passive capture wins while the account is in use.

| Account kind | Passive | Poll | Verified? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Claude subscription (`claude_code`) | SDK rate-limit events: `utilization`, `resets_at`, limit type | Subscription usage endpoint behind the same OAuth login | Passive is in the code today; the poll endpoint is checked in Phase 0 |
| ChatGPT subscription (`codex`) | Rate-limit fields on Codex responses | Codex usage endpoint behind the OAuth login | Both checked in Phase 0 |
| OpenRouter | Per-call cost in the response | Key and credits endpoints: limit, usage, remaining credit | Endpoints documented by OpenRouter; checked in Phase 0 |
| Anthropic or OpenAI API key | Rate-limit response headers | None for balance | Headers checked in Phase 0; balance shows as spend so far from CLIO's own ledger |
| vLLM, Ollama, llama.cpp, LM Studio, homelab router | Tokens from the call ledger | None | `unmetered`, with tokens served |
| Site endpoints (Argonne, AmSC) | Tokens from the call ledger | Whatever the site exposes, if anything | Per site; `unmetered` until one exists |

**CLIO's own credentials only.** Adapters use the credential the account was connected with. Unlike quotabubble, CLIO never reads another tool's credential files or keychain entries.

**Spend ledger.** The `provider.call_usage` audit rows already record tokens and cost per call. A rollup by account, session and agent gives spend for accounts with no balance endpoint and lets the person see which agent or study spent what.

**Failure.** A failed poll keeps the last good snapshot, dimmed and marked with its age, and records why. It never clears the value.

**Codex limit detection.** The text match in `codex/errors.py` is deleted and replaced by the structured fields the adapter reads, in line with the rule against prose matching.

## Design: selection

**Where a model can be named.** Every place that starts model work takes an optional `model`:

| Place | How |
| --- | --- |
| Root session | The person's picker, as today |
| Spawn tools | `spawn_agent_task(..., model=)` and per item in `spawn_agents_parallel` |
| Flows | `ctx.call(target, input, model=)`, and a class attribute for a flow's own default |
| Workflow steps | A `model` field on a step, editable by editors like any other field |
| Defined subagents | `Subagent(prefers=Prefers(model=..., provider=..., effort=...))` |
| Agents and plugins | `Prefers` and `Requires` on the class, as declared today |
| RLM leaves | `llm(query, context, model=)`, and the `rlm` subagent's own `Prefers` |
| Secondary roles | `summarizer` and any later role name a fleet entry instead of a separate provider config |

**A model reference** is either an exact `account/model` pair or a bare model id, which resolves to an account that serves it, preferring the caller's own account. `effort` maps onto the existing thinking levels.

**Resolution order** when a session or call starts:

1. An explicit `model` on the call.
2. The target's `Prefers` (subagent, then agent, then plugins in resolution order).
3. The caller's model, which is today's behaviour.

The first candidate is checked against the session's effective `Requires` and the fleet's `available` flag. An explicit model that fails the check is a typed refusal (`model_unavailable`, `model_requirement_unmet`) returned to the caller, so the model can pick another. A preference that fails moves to the next step, and the child records why.

**CLIO choosing.** The agent chooses by calling `list_models` and passing a `model`. Nothing picks a model behind its back. The `delegation.parent` fragment gains one line: name a model when a cheaper or larger one fits the subtask, and check `usage` first for long fan-outs.

**Recording.** Every session stores `model_choice`: what was asked, what ran, the source (`explicit`, `prefers`, `inherited`, `person`), and the reason for any step down the order. The Work view shows the model per row as an icon with details on hover, and export and provenance carry it.

**When a window runs out.** A plan-limit or credit rejection already arrives as a typed error. The session's next model call then follows one rule: if the person chose the model, CLIO asks through a Question with the alternatives the fleet offers; if CLIO or a preference chose it, the agent receives `model_exhausted` with the reset time and decides itself. There is never an automatic silent switch.

**Spending guard.** Settings gain a per-account switch, **CLIO may use this account for delegation**, on by default for subscriptions, local and free endpoints and off for metered and credit accounts. Choosing an account that is off raises a Question once per session. This keeps an agent from spending OpenRouter credit the person did not intend to spend.

**Cache.** A child's model is fixed when the child is created, so prompt caching inside a session is not broken by selection. Only the person switches a running root session's model.

## Design: agent tools and UI

**Tools**, in a `fleet` plugin that `core` requires, so every agent has them:

| Tool | Returns | Read-only |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `list_models(filter=None)` | Fleet entries the session may use: account, model, key capabilities, price, `available`, and a one-line usage summary. Filter by requirement, provider or billing kind | Yes |
| `usage(account=None)` | Usage snapshots: windows with percent and reset time, balance, age, spend by this session tree | Yes |
| `refresh_provider_models` | Unchanged; moves from `core` into `fleet` | No |

Results are compact by default, because a fleet with several local models can list dozens of entries. Both tools work from inside the `run_code` kernel, where filtering a long list is cheap.

**Usage view** ([#1802](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-agent/issues/1802)). A page in Settings, and a panel reachable from the chat footer, listing every connected account. Each row shows the provider icon, billing kind, a bar per window with its reset countdown, the balance for credit accounts, spend in this workspace, and health. Rows are grouped subscriptions first, then credit, metered and local. A toggle switches between percent used and percent remaining. A stale value is dimmed with its age on hover.

**Hover readout.** The tokens and cost readout under the chat box gains a hover card for the account the session runs on: its windows, reset times and balance, plus the tokens and cost this session and its children used. When a window passes 80% the readout shows a small marker, with no banner and no toast.

**Model in the Work view.** Each row carries a model icon; hover shows the `model_choice` record. A study or flow run can be read at a glance as "which branches ran on what".

**Usage on the flow railroad.** The railroad of a flow or workflow run carries a brief summary under its title: the models the run used, each with its share of the run's tokens and cost, and the windows of the accounts it ran on (for example `sonnet 61% · haiku 39% · Claude 5h window 42%`). Each box's hover adds the model it ran on and its `model_choice` source. People reading a run see what it cost and where without leaving it; the Usage view stays the place for every account.

**Desktop widget.** A quotabubble-style floating widget is a natural fit for the Tauri desktop app later. It reads `GET /v1/fleet` from any connected agent, including remote ones, so one widget can cover several agents. It is listed here so the endpoint is designed for it; building it is optional for 1.0.

## Open questions

Each has a proposed default so a plan can be written from this document.

| Question | Options | Proposed default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Can CLIO pick automatically, with no model named | An `auto` policy (cheapest model meeting `Requires`); only the agent choosing through `list_models` | Agent chooses. An `auto` policy hides a cost decision inside the runtime; revisit after 1.0 with evidence from `model_choice` records |
| Ordered preferences | `Prefers.model` as one id; as an ordered list | One id. A list becomes a maintained fallback list in code, which is what the model catalog work removed |
| Spending guard default | All accounts allowed; metered and credit accounts need consent | Subscriptions, local and free allowed; metered and credit need a Question once per session |
| Who owns a cross-account choice in a workflow | The editor that set it; the step's agent | Whoever wrote the step's `model` field; a step's own agent can still pass `model` to its spawns |
| Polling the Claude and Codex usage endpoints | Poll when idle; passive only | Poll when idle, every 5 minutes, only for accounts connected in CLIO, and only if Phase 0 confirms the endpoints are stable to call with our tokens |
| Budget limits | Per session token or dollar budgets on top of usage | Out of scope for this item. Flow limits already carry `budget_tokens`; dollar budgets come later |
| Remote agents | Each agent reports its own fleet; the desktop merges | Each agent serves its own `/v1/fleet`; the UI shows them grouped by agent, with no merge |
| Mid-session switch by the agent | Allow the agent to change its own model; only children get a choice | Only children. The agent forks or spawns onto another model instead, which keeps each transcript on one model |

## Phases and qualification

This item touches session creation and the spawn path, so it runs after the delegation plan lands and before RLM's Phase 3, which uses per-leaf model choice. The fleet and usage phases do not depend on delegation and can start now. Decisions use the prefix `M` in their own ledger.

1. **Phase 0: inventory and checks.** Confirm the Claude and Codex usage endpoints and their fields with real tokens; confirm OpenRouter's key and credits responses and the Anthropic and OpenAI rate-limit headers; list every hard-coded model list left in the code; map every place a child session gets its model.
2. **Phase 1: the fleet.** The read model, `GET /v1/fleet`, accounts with billing kind and health, entries joined with capabilities and price, deletion of the remaining hard-coded lists.
3. **Phase 2: usage.** The adapter protocol and `UsageSnapshot`, adapters for `claude_code`, `codex`, `openrouter`, `anthropic`, `openai` and an `unmetered` adapter for local and site endpoints, passive capture from the existing signals, idle polling, last-good handling, the spend rollup from `provider.call_usage`, and replacement of the Codex text match.
4. **Phase 3: selection.** `model` on spawn tools, `ctx.call`, workflow steps and `llm()`; `Prefers` applied at session creation; the resolution order and its typed refusals; `model_choice` recorded and exported; `model_exhausted` and the Question for person-chosen models; the spending guard; `summarizer` moved onto a fleet reference.
5. **Phase 4: tools and fragment.** The `fleet` plugin with `list_models` and `usage`, `refresh_provider_models` moved into it, and the `delegation.parent` line.
6. **Phase 5: UI.** Usage view, hover readout, model icon and `model_choice` hover in the Work view and railroad, and the railroad's usage summary. Verified with `ui_check.mjs` at 1440 by 900 and 390 by 844.
7. **Phase 6: qualification.**

| ID | Scenario | Passes when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M1 | Open the Usage view with Claude, Codex, OpenRouter and a local vLLM connected | Every account shows windows or balance with reset times; vLLM shows `unmetered` with tokens served |
| M2 | Hover the chat footer during a Claude session | The card shows the live window values from the SDK events, matching `usage()` |
| M3 | The agent calls `list_models`, then spawns a child on a smaller model | The child runs on that model; `model_choice` says `explicit` |
| M4 | A subagent declares `Prefers(model=...)` for a model that is not connected | The child runs on the parent's model and `model_choice` records the unmet preference |
| M5 | A spawn names a model without vision for a task whose plugins require vision | `model_requirement_unmet` is returned and nothing starts |
| M6 | A workflow with steps on three different models | Each step runs on its model; the railroad shows them; export carries them |
| M7 | A spawn on a metered OpenRouter model with the guard off | One Question; after approval the spawn runs, and a second spawn in the session does not ask again |
| M8 | A Claude window is exhausted mid-study in a child CLIO chose | The child's agent receives `model_exhausted` with the reset time and moves its work to another model |
| M9 | The same exhaustion on a person-chosen root model | A Question offers the fleet's alternatives; nothing switches until answered |
| M10 | A usage poll fails with the network down | The last good snapshot stays, dimmed with its age; the failure is recorded |
| M11 | RLM leaves with `model=` set to a cheaper model | Leaves run on that model and count in the spend rollup under the `rlm` node |
| M12 | A council run with members on two models | The railroad's summary names both models with their token shares and the account window; each member box's hover names its model and source |

**Done** when every phase is implemented, the Codex text match and the hard-coded model lists are gone, M1 to M12 pass against a freshly restarted stack with evidence in the ledger, and the endpoint checks from Phase 0 are recorded with their dates.

This plan turns three design documents into code. Agents become Python classes that select plugins. Plugins follow Agent Plugins 1.0.0 with CLIO content under `ai.iowarp.clio`. Orchestration becomes flows: DSPy modules whose calls are ordinary CLIO tasks. The blueprint system and the declared-workflow runner are deleted and replaced, not kept beside the new code.

## Contract

The designs in this folder are the contract. When code and design disagree, change the code. If the design itself turns out wrong, choose the fix that best keeps the design's intent, update the document in the same change, and record the decision in the acceptance ledger. The work runs to completion without stopping for review; the human reviews the finished branch.

| Document | Governs |
| --- | --- |
| [plugins-and-composition.md](plugins-and-composition.md) | Plugin format, packs, agents as plugin sets, resolution, coexistence rules, composed main prompt, trust |
| [agent-sdk.md](agent-sdk.md) | The Python classes, ownership, two-stage resolution, validation and `clio-agent plugin check` |
| [orchestration-semantics.md](orchestration-semantics.md) | Flows, the `ctx` primitives on the task layer, durability, plans, the `workflows.py` replacement |
| [model-fleet.md](model-fleet.md) | The fleet, usage, model selection at every spawn point, and the Usage UI (Phase 6) |
| [remote-agents-and-protocols.md](remote-agents-and-protocols.md) | Context only; out of scope for this change |

Base: `codex/agent-facing-async-tasks` in clio-agent (this setup branch sits on `55d06ee5`; the design review was done at `47b6bd49`), with gact-tui at the commit the submodule pins, which is on gact-tui's `codex/agent-facing-async-tasks`. That branch rebuilt the task layer. Read `docs/design/task-replacement-plan.md` and `docs/design/agent-facing-async-tasks.md` before Phase 1. When the team merges it, rebase onto `develop`.

## Rules

1. **Delete and replace.** Keep no dual loader, compatibility shim, feature flag or dormant copy of the blueprint system or the declared-workflow runner. A path judged wrong is deleted in the same change that replaces it. Do not stub anything listed as out of scope.
2. **The task layer is the only execution authority.** Flows submit through `Conversations.spawn`, task-capable MCP calls and Question tasks. They wait through `TaskOperations` and checkpoint in `TaskHistory`. Add no registry, store, scheduler or polling loop of your own.
3. **The model decides.** Follow the superseding principles in `.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Core never routes, completes or retries on a heuristic. A flow's control flow is code written by a plugin author or by the model, and core executes only what that code calls.
4. **No silent fallback.** Every refusal, stall or degraded path returns a typed reason that reaches the API and the trace.
5. **Repository rules.** Follow `AGENTS.md` for resource ownership and cleanup, ruff, tests and Conventional Commits. Do not touch the protected human files named in `task-replacement-plan.md`.
6. **Evidence over claims.** A phase is done when its ledger rows pass with recorded evidence: test names and results, and for UI work the screenshots you read.

## Out of scope

Do not implement, stub or reserve fields for these:

- Remote agents: `Peer`, `Expose`, A2A, ACP and Academy.
- Self-optimizing plugins: `evolved_from`, override slots, lessons and the optimizer gate.
- `rlm` and `code` flows, plus `run_code`. These depend on the separate programmatic tool calling work.
- Visual authoring of flows.

## Defaults for the open questions

Take these defaults and note each in the ledger.

| Open question | Default for this change |
| --- | --- |
| Task kind for flows | No new `TaskKind`. A flow run is checkpoints under its owning assignment, as declared workflows are now. |
| Handoff | Not implemented. Delegation returns a value. |
| Checkpoint size | Cap one run at 10,000 checkpoint entries and return a typed `flow_checkpoint_limit` outcome past it. |
| Context passed to subagents | The assignment prompt plus pinned evidence references (`input_task_refs`) the flow passes explicitly. |
| Plan or script by default | Plans only, since `run_code` is out of scope. |
| Edits from outside the plan | Only named editors may edit. The human cancels nodes through the existing task controls. |
| Naming | `flow` everywhere, because "loop" already means interval monitoring in CLIO. |

## Phase 0: inventory and removal manifest

No production code changes in this phase.

1. Map the blueprint system with production callers, using AST like the task replacement inventory did: `gact/agent_blueprints.py`, `gact/agent_blueprint_*.py`, `gact/blueprint_*.py`, `gact/expert_packs.py`, `gact/agents/blueprint_commission.py`, `gact/agents/execution_blueprint.py`, `gact/agents/unresolved_blueprint.py`, AGENT.md parsing, `clio-pack.yaml`, and their REST routes and GACT bindings.
2. Map the declared workflow: `gact/workflows.py`, `gact/workflow_state/`, `run_workflow` in `gact/task_declarations.py` and `gact/agents/spawn_runtime_declarations.py`, and module variants in `gact/agents/module_variants.py`.
3. Inventory `external/clio-agent-marketplace`. It has 28 AGENT.md agents. For each, record its experts, skills, MCP servers, A2UI catalogs, hooks and any `workflow:` block, and propose its plugin and pack split.

5. Commit, push the branch and open a draft PR, then continue straight to Phase 1. The manifest is for traceability, not a review gate.

## Phase 1: plugin standard, resolver and composed prompt

1. Add the public SDK package `clio_agent/sdk/` with `Plugin`, `Pack`, `Agent`, `Subagent`, `Flow`, `Requires`, `Prefers`, `PromptFile` and the `hook` decorator.
2. Add the plugin loader:
   - Read `plugin.json` against the Agent Plugins 1.0.0 schema, plus the `ai.iowarp.clio` extension.
   - Read the folder conventions: `skills/`, `mcp.json`, and `ai.iowarp.clio/` with `plugin.py`, `tools/`, `hooks/`, `subagents/`, `commands/`, `flows/`, `prompt/` and `a2ui/`.
   - Add one importer that brings Claude Code plugin layouts and marketplaces into the same internal record. clio-kit `main` is the main real-world example: 72 plugins in `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`, each with `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and some of `.mcp.json`, `skills/`, `hooks/hooks.json` and `agents/*.md`. It gets no special treatment. The importer maps that layout as follows:
     - A plugin whose only content is `dependencies` (such as `clio-hpc` or `clio-skills`) becomes a pack, so its members stay individually removable. `dependencies` on a plugin with content of its own become hard requirements.
     - `.mcp.json` entries become the plugin's MCP servers, started lazily.
     - `skills/` stays portable as is.
     - `hooks/hooks.json` events map onto CLIO hook events. An event with no CLIO equivalent is reported with a typed reason, never dropped silently. Other clients' hook files, such as `codex.json` or `opencode.js`, are ignored.
     - `agents/*.md` become defined subagents of that plugin. Claude Code tool names map to CLIO tools, and an unmappable tool is a typed import error. A `model:` pin becomes a model preference, not a requirement.
     - `federated-marketplaces.json` entries pinned by commit are followed as git sources and go through the trust step.
     - Client-specific index files outside the Claude Code format, such as `.clio-kit/catalogue.json`, are not read.
3. Trust:
   - pip-installed plugins are trusted.
   - Git and external marketplaces need an explicit trust step.
   - An update that changes executable parts needs the trust step again.
4. Resolution happens in two stages:
   - **Stage 1 (install):** `spec()` imports the agent once and stores a frozen spec with its checksum.
   - **Stage 2 (session start):** expand packs, apply the user delta, cascade removal of required plugins, and build the union of model requirements. Treat tool-name collisions and hook-ordering cycles as errors. Order hooks child to parent, adjustable with `before=`/`after=`. Compose the main prompt in its five sections, then pin the result to the session.
5. Add `clio-agent plugin check` and a pytest fixture that run the same resolver as install.
6. Create the `core` plugin. It holds:
   - the operating guidelines;
   - the rendering section generated from the UI catalog;
   - the `clio.runtime.tasks` lifecycle fragment;
   - the `react` flow wrapping `ClioReAct`.
7. Add the `Answer` hook event (`@hook("answer")` in the SDK, `Answer` in `hooks.json`). It fires once per turn on the settled answer, before the turn is saved. A hook may attach a note or a passed/failed check, shown under the answer and attributed to it, or return a revision. A revision lands visibly as a new answer part after a notice naming the hook and its reason; the original stays in the transcript, marked superseded. It is never a gate and never a silent swap, since the answer may already have streamed.

## Phase 2: migrate shipped agents and delete blueprints

1. Convert every marketplace agent to plugins, packs and Python agent classes on a branch of `iowarp/clio-agent-marketplace`. Cut the base agent's prompt apart into identity, `core` guidelines and one fragment per capability plugin.
2. Replace the blueprint REST routes and GACT bindings with plugin and agent routes.
3. In the same change, delete the AGENT.md loader, the `clio-pack.yaml` path and every module the manifest marks for removal. Add a guard test that rejects imports of the removed symbols.

## Phase 3: flows on the task layer

1. Add `Flow` as a `dspy.Module` with `forward(task, ctx)`. Implement `ctx.call`, `ctx.start`, `ctx.gather`, `ctx.as_completed`, `ctx.ask`, `ctx.step`, `ctx.workspace` and `ctx.depth` exactly as the orchestration document's table maps them onto the task layer.
2. Durability:
   - Derive invocation ids from the run, the call site, a hash of the target and input, and an occurrence index.
   - Pass each id to `spawn` so the handle is deterministic, and checkpoint the run through `TaskHistory`.
   - On replay, re-attach to existing handles.

3. Limits: enforce depth, concurrency, total model calls and budget in `ctx`, on top of the existing inference capacity.
4. Agents select a flow by id. `react` is the default.
5. Ship the `workflow` flow in `core`, with `Workflow`, `Step`, editors (`workflow_add_step`, `workflow_cancel_step`), growth bounds the caller or the person sets, and approval through a Question task. (Named `plan` until Phase 5, when it was renamed so it is not mistaken for Plan mode.)

7. Delete the declared-workflow runner, the `workflow:` parsing and its old `run_workflow` tool (the name now belongs to the orchestration plugin's tool for workflows as data). Move spawn-order merging and typed stalls into `ctx.gather` and the workflow flow.

## Phase 4: UI in gact-tui

Commit UI work in `external/gact-tui` on a branch of `iowarp/gact-tui`, and update the submodule pin in clio-agent.

1. Add the agent "+" menu. It adds and removes plugins, shows pack membership, previews the cascade when a required plugin is removed, and saves the result as a user agent (parent plus delta).
2. Show each plugin's provenance: core, standard, science, a pack, or the user.
3. Add a composed prompt view with each fragment attributed to its plugin.
4. Add a flow run view. It draws the live plan from task history, shows proposed nodes awaiting approval, and shows typed stalls with their reason.

Added Oct 23, 2026. The agent proposes an edit (`fs_propose_edit`) and the person applies it from the diff panel (`/diffs/apply`). That split comes from the older CLIO that held small models to deterministic pipelines. It also lets a write skip the PreToolUse hooks: proposing counts as read-only, and the person's apply runs no hooks. A plugin's write guard (WTF-P's, for one) therefore never sees a write.

1. The agent gets a write tool that changes the file on disk. It is not read-only, so the permission gate asks or allows by the session's mode, and PreToolUse hooks run on it like any other write. `Write` and `Edit` in Claude Code hooks match it.

## Decisions

| ID | Decision | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M-D1 | The design doc is the contract; its phases run as Phase 6 of the megachange plan. RLM leaves (M11) wait for the `rlm` flow, which the plan keeps out of scope. | The plan's scope rules |
| M-D2 | No polling adapter for the Claude subscription. Passive capture from `unifiedWindows` is the source, and an account with no recent call shows its last snapshot with its age. | Phase 0 found no usage endpoint reachable with CLIO's own credential, and passive capture already carries both windows |
| M-D3 | Usage snapshots live in an in-memory board (`USAGE_BOARD`), one per account, not a new store. After a restart an account shows "no reading yet" until its next call or read. | RULE 4: no fifth store; every value is a reading of a live window that the next call refreshes |
| M-D4 | OpenRouter's balance is read on demand when the fleet is read, at most once per `fleet.usage_poll_seconds` (300 s). No background poller. | Only the Usage view and `usage()` need it; a poller would spend calls nobody reads |
| M-D5 | A requirement on a fact the fleet does not report (a context size the provider never states) is recorded as `unverified` in `model_choice.reasons`, not refused. | Refusing on an unknown fact would block every local model; recording it keeps the decision visible |
| M-D6 | Spend is the sum of `Session.usage_by_model`, rolled up as each turn finishes. Sessions from before the rollup count under their pinned model and are listed as `estimated_sessions`. | Replaying transcripts to compute spend took the server to 2.3 GB RSS; the rollup is the session's own record |
| M-D7 | The spending guard covers models CLIO chooses for delegated work on an account the person has not allowed; it asks once per conversation (consent stored on the root session). | M-D8 | When the person's own model is exhausted, the turn's error card offers the fleet's alternatives (`switch_model`) and retries the turn on the one picked; nothing switches on its own. | M-D9 | The model picker keeps every model and shows a notice naming the models that fit the agent's requirements; sending on a model that misses one is refused with `model_requirement_unmet` (422). | Hiding rows made a missing model look disconnected; the refusal carries the reason |
| M-D10 | A run's model shares count tokens read and written, not cache reads. | Cache reads dominated and made a short synthesizer step look like most of the run |
| M-D11 | The line telling the agent to name a model for a subtask lives in the `fleet` plugin's `fleet.models` fragment, not a `delegation.parent` fragment. | No `delegation.parent` fragment exists under plugins; the fleet plugin owns the tools the line refers to, and `core` requires it |
| M-D12 | Rate-limit headers of Anthropic and OpenAI API keys are not captured yet (iowarp/clio-agent#1837); those accounts show spend from the session rollups. | lm15 reads response headers only on failed calls. A recording engine (`0aa21aa`) was reverted (`4237402`) because a custom `dspy.LM` engine bypasses DSPy's retry and stream recovery; a registered provider definition would instead lose DSPy's LiteLLM fallback. | Follow-up |
| M-D13 | `summarizer.provider`, `summarizer.api_base`, `summarizer.credential_ref`, `summarizer.transport`, `summarizer.model` and `summarizer.max_tokens` are deleted. | Nothing read them: the goal judge and the permission reviewer pass their own model, and a role on another account is chosen in `fleet.judges` as an account and model |
| M-D14 | A `Prefers(effort=...)` sets the child's thinking level after the message's own level and before the parent's. A preference naming only an effort applies to whichever model runs. | The design maps `effort` onto the thinking levels; a level the model cannot carry shows as unsupported in the turn's provenance |

{"path": "/home/user/clio-agent/.cloud-run/f17/ws-f17-docs/design/sdk/remote-agents-and-protocols.md", "size_bytes": 15968, "content": "# CLIO Remote Agents and Protocols

Oct 6, 2026 · @Jaime

A2A is the protocol CLIO should build peers and exposure on. Academy is supported natively, so agents running on DOE machines are first-class peers. The Agent Client Protocol connects editors to CLIO and lets CLIO drive local coding agents.

## What CLIO needs

CLIO reaches external agents in two ways. An `external-agents` pack lets any agent discover and call the agents a user has connected. A plugin can also declare **specific peers** it needs, such as a Tosca runner for the manufacturing plugin, and the user binds their address and credentials. Separately, an agent can **expose** itself to other systems.

The protocols are judged against five needs:

- **Long-running work.** HPC jobs run for hours to days, so a task must survive client disconnects and be reattached later.
- **One delegation interface.** A peer should look like a defined subagent to the root agent, whether it runs locally, in the cloud or at Argonne.
- **Runtime binding.** The agent names a peer; the operator supplies its address and credentials.
- **Firewalled compute nodes.** Peers on Aurora or Polaris often cannot accept inbound connections.
- **Exposure for free.** CLIO agents should be reachable by other systems from a tick mark, with their description generated from the resolved spec.

## A2A

A2A covers almost everything CLIO needs for agent-to-agent work, and its task model matches long-running HPC jobs better than anything else available. The current release is [spec v1.0.1](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/releases) (May 28, 2026), following v1.0.0 on March 12, 2026, the first major version with many breaking changes.

**Governance.** Google created A2A and donated it to the Linux Foundation, which [launched the project](https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-launches-the-agent2agent-protocol-project-to-enable-secure-intelligent-communication-between-ai-agents) on June 23, 2025. A Technical Steering Committee has one voting member each from Google, Microsoft, Cisco, AWS, Salesforce, ServiceNow, SAP and IBM ([GOVERNANCE.md](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/blob/main/GOVERNANCE.md)).

**Agent Card.** Published at `/.well-known/agent-card.json`. Required fields are `name`, `description`, `supportedInterfaces`, `version`, `capabilities`, `defaultInputModes`, `defaultOutputModes` and `skills`. Capabilities flag streaming, push notifications, extensions and an extended card that clients fetch after authenticating. Cards can be signed with JWS. This maps directly onto CLIO exposure: the card can be generated from the resolved spec.

**Tasks.** A Task carries status, artifacts and history. Messages and artifacts are made of Parts (text, raw bytes, URL or JSON data). The states are submitted, working, completed, failed, canceled, input-required, rejected and auth-required. `contextId` groups related tasks.

**Bindings.** JSON-RPC, gRPC and HTTP+JSON, with the same method names across them: `SendMessage`, `SendStreamingMessage`, `GetTask`, `ListTasks`, `CancelTask`, `SubscribeToTask`, push notification config methods and `GetExtendedAgentCard` ([specification](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/)).

**Long-running work.** Clients poll, stream over SSE, or receive webhooks. `SubscribeToTask` reattaches to a running task, and its first event is always the current Task snapshot. The spec calls itself designed for very long-running tasks, but it has no progress fields, no replay of missed stream events, optional webhook retries and implementation-defined retention.

**Auth.** API key, HTTP auth, OAuth2 (authorization code with PKCE, client credentials, device code), OpenID Connect and mutual TLS. A task can pause in auth-required to ask for credentials midway.

**Discovery.** Well-known URI, curated registries or direct configuration; no registry API is defined.

**SDK.** Python is [`a2a-sdk`](https://pypi.org/pypi/a2a-sdk/json) 1.2.2 (Oct 5, 2026), implementing spec 1.0 over all three bindings with a 0.3 compatibility mode.

## ACP

Two unrelated protocols share the abbreviation. The one for agent-to-agent communication is gone, merged into A2A. The one that matters for CLIO is the Agent Client Protocol, which connects editors to agents, so it is an exposure target and not a peer protocol.

**Agent Communication Protocol (IBM, BeeAI).** A REST protocol (`GET /agents`, `POST /runs`) with synchronous, streaming and background runs. IBM's team [announced the merger into A2A](https://github.com/orgs/i-am-bee/discussions/5) on August 25, 2025, archived [the repository](https://github.com/i-am-bee/acp) two days later, and stopped development; BeeAI users migrate through A2A adapters. CLIO should not build on it.

**Agent Client Protocol (Zed).** The editor equivalent of LSP: an editor talks to a coding agent over JSON-RPC, today on stdio, with Streamable HTTP still a draft proposal ([transports](https://agentclientprotocol.com/protocol/transports)). The agent implements `initialize`, `authenticate`, `session/new` and `session/prompt`, and streams `session/update` notifications with message chunks, tool calls and plans. The client implements permission requests, and optionally file system, terminal and elicitation methods.

Adoption is broad: the [clients page](https://agentclientprotocol.com/overview/clients) lists Zed, JetBrains, Neovim, Emacs, VS Code and others, and [41 agents](https://agentclientprotocol.com/overview/agents) including Claude Agent, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI and GitHub Copilot. The Python SDK is [`agent-client-protocol`](https://pypi.org/project/agent-client-protocol/) (stable 0.12.1, with 1.0.0 release candidates in September 2026); protocol version is 1.

For CLIO this means one more exposure tick mark: `Expose(acp=True)` would let any of those editors drive a CLIO agent, with ACP's permission requests mapped onto CLIO grants. Because the transport is local stdio, it suits CLIO running on the user's machine, not a remote peer.

In the other direction, the `acp` plugin in the `external-agents` pack lets CLIO drive any of those local coding agents, such as Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI, as subagents over stdio.

A third ACP, the Agentic Commerce Protocol from Stripe and OpenAI, covers checkout flows and is not relevant.

## Academy

Academy is the strongest option for agents that live on DOE machines, but it is a Python actor framework rather than an agent protocol, so CLIO supports it natively through an adapter. It comes from Globus Labs (University of Chicago and Argonne), is MIT licensed, and reached [`academy-py` 1.0.0](https://pypi.org/project/academy-py/) on September 8, 2026.

**Agent model.** Agents subclass `Agent`, expose remotely callable `@action` methods, and run autonomous `@loop` methods until shutdown ([concepts](https://docs.academy-agents.org/stable/concepts/)). Callers hold a `Handle` and await action results directly. Messaging is request and response only; pub/sub and streaming actions are open issues.

**Exchanges.** Agents reach each other through an exchange: local, Redis, a hybrid of direct TCP with Redis fallback for peers behind NAT or firewalls, or an HTTP exchange using SSE, with a hosted instance at exchange.academy-agents.org. The HTTP exchange authenticates with Globus OAuth tokens. Agents discover one another through the exchange's query methods.

**HPC deployment.** A `Manager` launches agents onto any executor, including Parsl and Globus Compute ([HPC guide](https://docs.academy-agents.org/stable/guides/hpc/)). The [Academy paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.05428v2) ran agents on Aurora and Polaris, reporting 5.5 ms warm starts and about 385 µs action latency, with case studies in materials discovery (MOFA) and decentralized learning across more than 1,500 agents. Persistent agents can outlive the application that launched them.

**LLM and protocol integration.** The [LLM guide](https://docs.academy-agents.org/stable/guides/llm/) shows agents wrapped as LangChain tools by hand, since handles carry no docstrings or signatures, and an MCP plug-in lives in a separate extensions repository. No A2A support was found.

**Limits as a CLIO peer.**

- Python only, with pickle as the default serialization (alternatives since 0.5.0).
- No streaming or progress events, only request and response.
- Globus Auth consent prompts and 48-hour token expiry need refresh handling for long runs.
- Fault tolerance is left to the application.
- Action descriptions for an LLM must be supplied by hand.

## Comparison

Only A2A serves as a general peer protocol; Academy covers HPC-resident agents and the Agent Client Protocol covers editors.

| Property | A2A | Academy | Agent Client Protocol |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Role for CLIO | Peers and exposure | Peers on DOE machines | Exposure to editors; driving local coding agents |
| Status | Spec 1.0.1, Linux Foundation | 1.0.0, Globus Labs | Protocol v1, community |
| Transport | JSON-RPC, gRPC, HTTP+JSON | Exchange: Redis, TCP, HTTP+SSE | JSON-RPC on stdio; HTTP in draft |
| Long-running tasks | Task states, resubscribe with snapshot, webhooks | Persistent agents; request/response only | Session-scoped |
| Streaming | SSE | Not yet | `session/update` notifications |
| Behind firewalls | Needs a reachable endpoint; webhooks hard on compute nodes | Hybrid and HTTP exchanges relay through the exchange | Local process only |
| Self-description | Signed Agent Card with skills | Discovery queries; no LLM-ready descriptions | `initialize` capabilities |
| Auth | OAuth2, OIDC, API key, mTLS | Globus OAuth | `authenticate` method |
| Language | Six official SDKs | Python only | Rust, TypeScript, Python, Java, Kotlin |

## Design for CLIO

External agents are reached through plugins, like every other capability. The `external-agents` pack gives an agent discovery and delegation over A2A, ACP and Academy, and a plugin that always needs a specific peer declares it. The agent itself owns only its exposure.

```python
# manufacturing plugin, ai.iowarp.clio/peers/
tosca_runner = Peer("tosca-runner", protocol="a2a",
                    skills=["topology optimization"])
aurora_sim = Peer("aurora-sim", protocol="academy",
                  actions={"run_case": "Run one simulation case and return its outputs"})

# the agent owns only its exposure
class Factorio(ScienceAgent):
    plugins = ScienceAgent.plugins + ["manufacturing@^1"]
    expose = Expose(a2a=True, acp=True)
```

```yaml
# operator binding, never in the agent definition
peers:
  tosca-runner:
    card: https://<host>/.well-known/agent-card.json
    auth: oauth2-client-credentials
  aurora-sim:
    exchange: globus
    agent: <academy agent id>
```

**Discovery, not fragments.** Peers describe themselves: A2A through Agent Cards, Academy through exchange discovery queries. No peer contributes a prompt fragment. The `external-agents` pack contributes one, telling the agent it has tools to discover and delegate to the agents the user has connected, conditional on which protocol plugins are present. Because Academy handles carry no descriptions, an Academy peer's actions are described in its declaration.

**One delegation interface.** The root agent delegates to `tosca-runner` exactly as it would to a defined subagent. Results come back as CLIO artifacts and events, whichever protocol carried them.

**Binding is a requirement.** A peer declared by a plugin is required configuration. The UI asks the user for its address and credentials, and the session does not start until the binding is filled or the plugin that needs it is removed. At session start the runtime fetches each bound peer's Agent Card, or queries the Academy exchange, and checks that the declared skills or actions are present.

**Location.** The agent never fixes where a peer runs. It may state a preference, such as `prefers=Prefers(locality="hpc")`, the same way it states model preferences; the operator decides.

**Long-running tasks.** A peer call is an external task in CLIO's task layer. It returns a handle at acceptance and is observed, waited on and cancelled with the same task controls as any other work, and its result reaches the caller through the mailbox. CLIO stores the A2A task id and `contextId` as the task's backend reference, polls or resubscribes from the server side, and treats the snapshot returned on resubscribe as the source of truth. An observed terminal state settles as externally acknowledged; lost visibility stays uncertain rather than becoming a failure, and an uncertain submission is never sent again. Webhooks are not used toward compute nodes, since they rarely accept inbound connections. Because A2A defines no progress fields, CLIO reads progress from status messages and partial artifacts.

**Academy peers.** An adapter turns an Academy handle into a CLIO external task with the same controls. With no streaming, the task reports working until the action returns. Action descriptions come from the `Remote` declaration, since Academy handles carry none, and Globus refresh tokens live in the operator's credentials to survive the 48-hour expiry.

**Exposure.** `Expose(a2a=True)` publishes an Agent Card generated from the resolved spec: the role becomes the description, and plugins and defined subagents become skills. The card is signed with the deployment's key. `Expose(acp=True)` ships a local stdio adapter so editors can drive the agent, mapping permission requests onto CLIO grants.

**Trust.** Everything a peer returns is data, never instructions to the agent, the same boundary that applies to tool results.

## Decisions from review

- **Academy is supported natively.** CLIO is a science platform, and agents on DOE machines should be first-class peers rather than reached through a second protocol.
- **Missing peers block the session.** A required binding is surfaced in the UI for the user to fill; the agent does not silently run without it.
- **Peers are discovered, not described in the prompt.** Only the `external-agents` pack contributes a fragment.
- **Specific peers belong to plugins.** Agents own only their exposure.
- **Progress for long jobs is not available** through A2A, and CLIO accepts that.
- **ACP exposure is local only** until Streamable HTTP lands in the Agent Client Protocol.
